source.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Wei Jie Yeo; Nirmalendu Prakash; Clement Neo; Roy Ka-Wei Lee; Erik Cambria; Ranjan Satapathy

record.tranche_reason: The study causally intervenes on SAE features related to refusal and harm. Its results refine the single-direction account by separating harmful features from refusal features and identifying a shared refusal-related feature subset.
record.gate_note: The study uses a difference-in-means refusal direction to restrict and rank SAE features, and compares activation steering (AS) with feature interventions. Values in Figures 2, 3, and 9 are not given numerically in the text and are recorded as figure only. Hyperparameter choices and feature-selection statistics are not recorded as outcomes. The cited findings from prior work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: It uses a different method, SAE feature interventions guided by the difference-in-means direction, on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B chat models. Its results bear on V5: harm features act upstream of a separate refusal feature set (Tables 1–2, Fig. 3). They bear on V3: jailbreaks and suffixes suppress refusal features (Tables 2–3). It also reports the direction-ablation (AS) baseline with capability tables for V1 (Tables 5–6). It does not argue the single-direction account is wrong; AS is treated as the upper bound.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate SAE feature sets, with harm features causally upstream of refusal features. Jailbreaks (paraphrases, suffix trigger tokens) work by suppressing refusal features. Refusal features also improve OOD classification of adversarial prompts.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means refusal directions to guide SAE feature selection, then applies feature-level interventions rather than ablating or adding the single direction itself; compares against activation steering.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effects differ by model and feature subset: specific-feature clamping is largely ineffective for Llama, Gemma and Llama differ in harmful-feature changes, and suffix suppression is lower for Llama. The authors also report greater intervention sensitivity for Llama in some capability evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: A sparse probe on refusal features separates jailbroken adversarial prompts from vanilla harmful ones far better than dense probes (Table 4, gap 0.03 vs 0.32 in Gemma, 0.17 vs 0.93 in Llama).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction-aligned features give OOD-robust detection of adversarial harmful prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-feature activations concentrate on the final chat-template tokens; omitting them drops refusal-feature activation sharply (Fig. 7, A.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal is read out at post-instruction template tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Only two chat models are studied. Several refusal and jailbreak outcomes are reported in figures without numerical values in the text. Feature interventions use selected SAE features and layers rather than the single direction across every layer and position. The paper notes that its small feature-set size may omit relevant features and that selection depends on the refusal direction.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the OOD probe results in Table 4 because the reported classifier scores measure classification performance on adversarial examples, not refusal behavior or the causal effect of refusal-direction ablation. Other plotted feature-search comparisons and capability results for alternative feature-search methods were not included because they are not outcomes of the single-direction intervention.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal (only SAE feature activation was tested). Numeric jailbreak rates for AS.
Training against ablation for robustness. Suppression of the direction itself rather than SAE features.
All; no affine, cone or multi-direction geometry is tested.
All; base-to-chat SAE transfer is about reconstruction, not transfer of the direction.

missing.what: Mean cosine similarity to the refusal direction: refusal features 0.23 versus harm features 0.19.
Per-token suffix suppression of refusal features, and the reduced added effect of harm clamping after trigger tokens such as 'fictional'.
Model refusal rates on GPT-4o-converted harmful versions of jailbreak prompts (38%/42%); these define the analysed sample.

record.verdict_notes: The subjects are Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B; the record's 'GEMMA-22B' and '22B' are wrong. Table 1 values for the FH conditions look column-swapped in the record; recheck against the PDF. AS ablation numbers appear only in figures. Harm and refusal feature sets are defined partly by construction (common versus category-specific features), which weakens the V5 evidence somewhat. V4 links were removed because SAE feature subsets are not a geometric test of refusal.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether projecting one direction out of every layer and position is sufficient across safety-trained chat models generally. Its feature interventions use selected SAE features and selected layers; capability evaluation is limited to the reported tasks.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The study examines activation changes associated with jailbreak prompts and suffixes, but does not train models against refusal-direction ablation.
The study distinguishes SAE feature sets, not affine subspaces or cones, and does not establish a complete geometric account of refusal.
The separation is tested using selected SAE feature sets and interventions in two models; it is not established across model families or training procedures.

The study does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages or model variants. Its base-SAE/chat-model evaluation concerns SAE reconstruction and is not a test of behavioral transfer of the direction.
No comparison of refusal training methods or training stages is reported.
No reasoning-model refusal-direction test is reported.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on V1 (AS baseline: jailbreak upper bound and capability), V3 (refusal-feature suppression by jailbreaks and suffixes) and V5 (Sect. 4.2 'Does LLM represent Harm and Refusal Separately?').

tranche.reason: Different method (SAE features selected by cosine to the DiM direction, then attribution patching and clamping) aimed at how refusal is mediated. It also reports its own AS baseline results. It does not argue a version is wrong, so T5 does not apply.

source_check.notes: All Gemma rows say 22B; the model is Gemma-2-2B, which affects the size buckets. Table 1 values are swapped in H2/H4/H6/H8 (suppression 0.48/0.51; P(I) drop 0.71/0.37). Not recorded: GCG was ineffective on both models, WildJailbreak ASR is 70% for both, and FR features have only mean cosine 0.23 to the direction (FH 0.19). EMNLP venue is not in the arXiv v1 text.

statements.problem: none. EMNLP venue is not stated in the arXiv v1 text.

statements.correction: 2505.23556: AdvSuffixes suppress FR by 0.72 (Gemma-2-2B) vs 0.35 (Llama-3.1-8B). No suffix ASR is reported. Llama's suffix suppression (0.35) is near its successful WildJailbreak FR drop (0.40). The SAEs differ: Gemma Scope (JumpReLU, x32) vs Llama Scope (TopK, x8). GCG was ineffective on both models.
statements.problem: This study gives no ASR for the suffix attacks, so it shows uneven suppression, not uneven attack success. Here Gemma is the stronger case, yet the conditions group Gemma with the weak families. The two models also use different SAEs.

statements.correction: Optional detail: FR features have mean cosine 0.23 with the refusal direction (FH 0.19), per App. A.1.

statements.problem: none. Caveat: model family is confounded with the SAE used (Gemma Scope vs Llama Scope).

statements.correction: Models: Gemma-2-2B (2B) and Llama-3.1-8B, so the range is 2-14B. Table 1: FH clamp suppresses FR by 0.48 (Gemma; random 0.05) and 0.51 (Llama; random 0.19). P(I) drops by 0.71 and 0.37 (random 0.06, 0.04). In Llama, clamping Fspecific alone is largely ineffective; Fcommon jailbreaks (Fig. 3, figure-only).
statements.problem: The conditions give a '4-14B' range, but this study's Gemma-2-2B is 2B. The cited rows H2 and H4 carry swapped Table 1 values.

statements.correction: Gemma-2-2B: FH falls 0.49 (DS) and 0.30 (DF); FR falls 0.73 (DS) and 0.18 (DF). App. A.7: adversarial paraphrases obscure harmful verbs, and token-sensitive SAE features may explain the FH decrease; FR falls even more. Authors: the differences sit mainly on final chat tokens, so harm features 'may also directly influence' refusal. Llama: FH 0.10 (DS), 0.05 (DF).
statements.problem: It omits the authors' alternative explanation for the Gemma FH drop. The failed-jailbreak FH drop (0.30) happens while the model still refuses, so it does not show harm-refusal entanglement.

statements.correction: Gemma-2-2B: FH relative drop of 0.49 in successful vs 0.30 in failed jailbreaks (WildJailbreak, compared with GPT-4o explicit paraphrases). FR drops more (0.73). App. A.7 attributes the FH decrease possibly to obscured harmful verbs.
statements.problem: The study shows FH roughly halved, not lost. It also falls 0.30 in failed jailbreaks, and the authors offer a paraphrase/token-sensitivity explanation, so the conflict is weaker than framed.

statements.correction: 2505.23556's causal tests (feature clamping) are on Gemma-2-2B (2B) and Llama-3.1-8B (8B), so the range is 2-9B. Its 10-100B entry should move to 1-10B.
statements.problem: The misparse diagnosis is right (GEMMA-22B is Gemma-2-2B), but 'causal tests ... on 4-9B models' leaves out this study's 2B model.
